content: 1. The administration of lisinopril alongside propranolol or hydrochlorothiazide does not result in any clinically significant pharmacokinetic interactions. 2. The bioavailability of lisinopril is not affected by the presence of food in the stomach. 3. Lisinopril reduces potassium loss caused by thiazide-type diuretics. However, the concurrent use of potassium-sparing agents (e.g., spironolactone, triamterene, or amiloride), potassium supplements, or potassium-containing salt substitutes may lead to significant increases in serum potassium levels. 4. If the use of these agents is necessary due to demonstrated hypokalemia, they should be used cautiously with frequent monitoring of serum potassium levels. 5. Potassium-sparing agents are generally not recommended for patients with heart failure who are receiving lisinopril. 6. Lithium toxicity has been reported in patients taking lithium concurrently with drugs that promote sodium elimination, including ACE inhibitors. 7. Lithium toxicity is typically reversible upon discontinuation of both lithium and the ACE inhibitor. 8. Frequent monitoring of serum lithium levels is recommended when lisinopril is administered concurrently with lithium. 9. Thiazides may reduce arterial responsiveness to norepinephrine, but not to a degree that would prevent the therapeutic effectiveness of pressor agents. 10. Thiazides may enhance the responsiveness to tubocurarine. 11. The diuretic, natriuretic, and antihypertensive effects of thiazide diuretics may be diminished when administered concurrently with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The impact of NSAIDs on the antihypertensive effects of fosinopril sodium and hydrochlorothiazide has not been studied. 12. By alkalinizing the urine, hydrochlorothiazide may reduce the effectiveness of methenamine. 13. The absorption of hydrochlorothiazide is impaired in the presence of anionic exchange resins such as cholestyramine and colestipol. Single doses of these resins can bind hydrochlorothiazide and reduce its gastrointestinal absorption by up to 85% and 43%, respectively. 14. Long-term studies in rats and mice receiving hydrochlorothiazide at doses up to 100 mg/kg/day (rats) and 600 mg/kg/day (mice) revealed no evidence of carcinogenicity in rats or female mice. However, there was equivocal evidence of hepatocarcinogenicity in male mice. 15. Hydrochlorothiazide was not genotoxic in in vitro assays using various strains of Salmonella typhimurium (Ames assay), the Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) test for chromosomal aberrations, or in in vivo assays using mouse germinal cell chromosomes, Chinese Hamster bone marrow chromosomes, and the Drosophila sex-linked recessive lethal trait gene. 16. Positive test results were observed in the in vitro CHO Sister Chromatid Exchange (clastogenicity) test and the Mouse Lymphoma Cell (mutagenicity) assays using hydrochlorothiazide concentrations of 43 to 1300 mg/mL. Positive results were also obtained in the Aspergillus nidulans nondisjunction assay using unspecified concentrations of hydrochlorothiazide. 17. No adverse effects on fertility were observed in rats and mice receiving dietary hydrochlorothiazide prior to mating and throughout gestation at doses up to 4 mg/kg/day (rats) and 100 mg/kg/day (mice). 18. Lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide are classified as Pregnancy Category D by the FDA for the second and third trimesters and Category C for the first trimester. Refer to warnings regarding fetal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. 19. There is no Australian Drug Evaluation Committee (ADEC) guidance on the use of lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide in pregnant women. 20. There is no FDA guidance on the use of lisinopril/hydrochlorothiazide during labor and delivery. 21. It is unknown whether lisinopril is excreted in human milk. However, radioactive studies in lactating rats have shown the presence of lisinopril in milk at levels similar to plasma concentrations. Thiazides are known to appear in human milk. 22. Due to the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants from ACE inhibitors and hydrochlorothiazide, a decision should be made to either discontinue nursing or discontinue the drug, considering the importance of the medication to the mother. 23. The safety and effectiveness of lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide in pediatric patients have not been established. 24. Clinical studies of lisinopril and hydrochlorothiazide did not include sufficient numbers of subjects aged 65 and older to determine whether they respond differently from younger subjects. However, other reported clinical experience has not identified differences in responses between elderly and younger patients.
